title: Highway planning and survey
summary: Nepal Road Standard 2070 is the code that governs here, and its two classifications must be kept apart — the FUNCTIONAL classes (H, F, D, U) and the TERRAIN classes (plain, rolling, mountainous, steep), because the same functional class carries very different geometric standards in different terrain. For surveys, the home interview method is the answer for a large urban area because it alone captures internal trips, purpose and socio-economic data, which are what allow trip generation to be forecast rather than merely described.

sections.heading: Road classification
sections.body:
**Nepal Road Standard 2070 — the FUNCTIONAL classification:**

| Class | Designation | Function |
|---|---|---|
| **National Highway** | **H** | The main **arterial** routes across the country (e.g. **H01, the Mahendra Highway**) |
| **Feeder Road** | **F** | Connects **district headquarters and economic centres** to the highways |
| **District Road** | **D** | Traffic **within a district** |
| **Urban Road** | **U** | Within **municipal** areas |

**The TERRAIN classification** — and this is the one that actually sets the geometric standards:

| Terrain | Cross slope of the country |
|---|---|
| **Plain** | **Up to 10%** |
| **Rolling** | **10 – 25%** |
| **Mountainous** | **25 – 60%** |
| **Steep** | **Over 60%** |

**The two classifications are independent, and confusing them is the standard error.** A National Highway in **plain** terrain is designed for **120 km/h**; the same National Highway in **steep** terrain may be designed for **40 km/h** or less. The functional class states the road's **importance and role**; the terrain class states what is **physically achievable**.

**Design speeds (NRS 2070), by class and terrain:**

| Class | Plain | Rolling | Mountainous | Steep |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **National Highway** | **100 – 120** | 80 – 100 | **50 – 60** | **40 – 50** |
| Feeder Road | 80 – 100 | 60 – 80 | 40 – 50 | 30 – 40 |
| District Road | 60 – 80 | 50 – 60 | 30 – 40 | 25 – 30 |

Each cell gives a **ruling** and a **minimum** design speed: the ruling value is used wherever the terrain permits, and the minimum only where it does not — and the departure must be justified and documented rather than adopted for convenience.

**Classification by surface type** is a **construction description**, not a classification of function — a distinction questions test:

| Surface | Character |
|---|---|
| **Earthen** | Formation only; passable in dry weather |
| **Gravelled** | A granular wearing course |
| **Blacktopped (bituminous)** | Sealed surface |
| Concrete | Rigid pavement |

A road can be a **National Highway that is gravelled**, or a **District Road that is blacktopped** — the two descriptions are orthogonal.

**Road width terms**, from narrow to wide, and they are examined directly:

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Carriageway** | The **paved travel surface** — **3.5 m per lane** (3.75 m for a single-lane national highway) |
| **Roadway (formation) width** | Carriageway **plus the shoulders** |
| **Right of way (ROW)** | The **whole acquired land corridor**, including drains, slopes and provision for future widening |

**Typical values (NRS 2070):**

| Class | Carriageway | Formation width (mountainous) | ROW |
|---|---|---|---|
| National Highway | 7.0 m (2 lanes) | 8.5 – 11 m | 25 – 50 m |
| Feeder Road | 5.5 – 7.0 m | 6.5 – 8.5 m | 20 – 30 m |
| District Road | 3.75 – 5.5 m | 4.5 – 6.5 m | 15 – 20 m |

**Reserving an adequate right of way is the cheapest provision a road project can make**, and the most often neglected. Acquiring land after development has occurred alongside the road costs many times what it would have cost at the outset, and in a built-up area may be impossible — which is why widening an existing urban road is so much more expensive than building a new one.

**The Indian classification (Nagpur plan)** is also examinable, since much Nepali practice derives from IRC:

| Class | Function |
|---|---|
| **National Highway (NH)** | Main arterial routes |
| **State Highway (SH)** | Within a state, connecting to NHs |
| **Major District Road (MDR)** | Within a district |
| **Other District Road (ODR)** | Lower-order district roads |
| **Village Road (VR)** | Village to the nearest higher-class road |

**The Indian road development plans**, in order:

| Plan | Period | Pattern | Density target |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Nagpur** | **1943 – 61** | **Star and grid** | **16 km/100 km²** |
| **Bombay** | **1961 – 81** | **Square grid** | **32 km/100 km²** |
| **Lucknow** | **1981 – 2001** | — | **82 km/100 km²** |

The **Nagpur plan** introduced the five-class hierarchy above and the **Nagpur formula** for road length from the numbers of towns and villages to be served. Note that **radial and circular** is an **urban** pattern for a city radiating from a centre — not a national plan pattern, and it appears as a distractor for the Nagpur question.

sections.heading: Highway alignment
sections.body:
**Requirements of an ideal alignment**, in the conventional order:

> **SHORT · EASY · SAFE · ECONOMICAL**

| Requirement | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Short** | The shortest route reduces construction, maintenance and vehicle operating cost |
| **Easy** | Easy to construct and maintain, and easy for vehicles to negotiate — moderate gradients and curves |
| **Safe** | Adequate sight distance, gentle curves, stable slopes |
| **Economical** | Lowest **total** cost — construction plus maintenance plus vehicle operating cost over the design life |

**These requirements conflict**, and recognising that is the substance: the **shortest** route in hill country is usually the **steepest** and least easy; the **easiest** gradient requires a long, winding alignment that is not short. The design resolves the conflict by economics — minimising the **total transport cost**, not the construction cost alone.

**Obligatory points** — the constraint that shapes any real alignment:

| Type | Examples |
|---|---|
| **Points through which the alignment MUST pass** | A **bridge site** (the narrowest, most stable river crossing), a **mountain pass** (the lowest saddle), an intermediate **town** to be served, an existing junction |
| **Points the alignment must AVOID** | A **marsh or lake**, **unstable ground and landslide zones**, a **religious or cultural site**, a forest or protected area, **expensive built-up land**, a burial ground |

**In Nepal the avoid-list is dominated by geology**: **landslide-prone slopes, active faults, debris flow fans and unstable colluvium**. An alignment chosen for its geometry and then found to cross an active slide is a project that will fail — and the failure will recur annually, not once. This is why the **geological and geotechnical survey** is not a formality but the survey that most affects the alignment.

**Factors controlling alignment:**

| Factor | Influence |
|---|---|
| **Obligatory points** | The framework within which the alignment is chosen |
| **Traffic** | Origin–destination pattern, and the desire lines it reveals |
| **Geometric design** | Gradient, radius, sight distance limits |
| **Economics** | Total transport cost |
| **Other considerations** | Drainage, water table, geology, land use, monotony, environmental and social impact |

**Special problems of a HILL road alignment** — the Nepali case, and each item is a genuine design driver:

| Consideration | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Stability of slopes** | The alignment must cross stable ground; avoid colluvium, old slides, steep cut faces in weak rock |
| **Drainage** | **Water is the enemy**; the alignment must permit cross drainage and must not concentrate flow |
| **Gradient** | Ruling **5%**, limiting **7%**, exceptional **10%** in mountainous terrain; **hairpin bends limited to 4%** |
| **Resisting length** | The total "work" of the rise; kept within limits so vehicles are not overtaxed |
| **Curvature** | Minimum radii; hairpin bends where the slope must be climbed |
| **Balance of cut and fill** | Minimises spoil disposal, which is itself an environmental hazard |
| **Number of hairpin bends** | Minimised; each is a hazard and a cost |
| **Avoiding excessive rise and fall** | Ups and downs waste climb already gained |

**Spoil disposal deserves emphasis** because it is where hill road construction does most of its environmental damage: **tipping excavated material down the slope** buries fields and forest, blocks streams, and loads the slope below with unstable debris that fails in the next monsoon. The correct practice — **designed spoil tips at identified stable locations, with retaining structures and drainage** — costs money and is routinely omitted. It is a clear case where the engineering and the environmental obligation coincide.

**Engineering surveys for a new alignment**, in sequence:

| Stage | Purpose | Output |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Map (desk) study** | Identify possible routes from topographic maps, satellite imagery and geological maps | Alternative corridors |
| **2. Reconnaissance survey** | Walk or fly the alternatives; broad assessment of terrain, geology, drainage and obligatory points | The preferred corridor |
| **3. Preliminary survey** | Detailed survey of the chosen corridor; compare alternative alignments within it; preliminary geometric design and cost | The selected alignment |
| **4. Final location and detailed survey** | Peg the centre line; detailed levels, cross-sections, drainage, soil and material surveys | Drawings, quantities, estimate |

**The reconnaissance survey is where the largest savings are made or lost**, because it selects the corridor — and no amount of refinement at stage 4 can recover a corridor chosen through unstable ground. A day spent walking the ground with a geologist at reconnaissance is worth more than a month of detailed survey afterwards.

Instruments and methods now used: **total station and GNSS** for the detailed survey, **satellite imagery and digital elevation models** for the desk study, and increasingly **UAV (drone) photogrammetry** for the preliminary survey — which is particularly valuable in Nepal, where walking a corridor may take days and the terrain is often inaccessible.

sections.heading: Traffic surveys and studies
sections.body:
**Traffic surveys establish what the road must carry**, and each answers a different question:

| Survey | Answers |
|---|---|
| **Traffic volume** | **How many** vehicles, of what type, when |
| **Origin–destination (O–D)** | **Where** trips begin and end |
| **Spot speed** | How **fast** traffic travels at a point |
| **Speed and delay** | Where the **delays** occur on a journey |
| **Parking** | Demand and supply of parking |
| **Accident** | Where and why accidents occur |

**Traffic volume study.** Counts are expressed in **PCU (Passenger Car Units)**, because Nepali and Indian traffic is highly mixed and a count in vehicles is meaningless:

| Vehicle | PCU factor |
|---|---|
| **Car, taxi, light van** | **1.0** |
| Motorcycle, scooter | 0.5 |
| **Bus, truck** | **3.0** |
| Tractor-trailer | 4.5 |
| Bicycle | 0.5 |
| Cycle rickshaw | 2.0 |
| Animal-drawn cart | 6.0 – 8.0 |
| Hand cart | 3.0 |

**PCU factors depend on the road and the flow**, being higher on a narrow road and at high flows — because a slow heavy vehicle obstructs more when overtaking is difficult. IRC 106 gives values by situation.

**Derived volume measures:**

| Measure | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **ADT / AADT** | **Average (Annual) Daily Traffic** — the basis of pavement design |
| **Peak hour volume** | The design volume for **capacity and geometry** |
| **Design hourly volume (DHV)** | Usually the **30th highest hourly volume** of the year |
| Directional split | The proportion in the heavier direction |
| **Traffic composition** | The share of each vehicle class — governs the **VDF** for pavement design |

**The 30th highest hourly volume** deserves explanation: designing for the **highest** hour of the year would be uneconomical, since that hour occurs once; designing for the average hour would leave the road congested much of the time. The 30th highest is the conventional compromise — exceeded on only 29 hours in the year.

**Origin–destination study.** Its purpose is to establish **desire lines** — where the demand actually is, which is not necessarily where roads exist.

| Method | How | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| **HOME INTERVIEW** | Household survey, on a **1–10% sample** | **LARGE URBAN AREAS**; comprehensive planning |
| **Road-side interview** | Drivers questioned at a station | **Through traffic**; bypass studies |
| **Registration number** | Numbers recorded at entry and exit, then matched | **CORDON** studies; quick and cheap |
| **Tag on vehicle** | A card fixed at entry, collected at exit | Small areas, short duration |
| Return post card | Cards handed out, returned by post | Cheap, but **low response rate** |
| License plate video / ANPR | Automated | Modern equivalent of the registration method |

**Why the home interview method is the answer for a large urban area** — it alone captures what the others cannot:

| It captures | Why that matters |
|---|---|
| **ALL trips, including those wholly INSIDE the study area** | Roadside methods catch only vehicles crossing a survey station |
| **Trip PURPOSE** — work, education, shopping, social | Essential to modelling; purpose determines how the trip responds to change |
| **SOCIO-ECONOMIC data** — income, vehicle ownership, household size | The variables that **EXPLAIN** trip generation, and so allow it to be **FORECAST** |
| **ALL modes**, including walking and public transport | Roadside interviews sample vehicles, not people |

**That third row is decisive.** Only household data lets trip generation be **modelled and forecast** — a roadside survey describes today's traffic but cannot predict tomorrow's, because it does not know why the trips are made or who makes them. Its cost is that it is **expensive and slow**, which is why it is done on a sample.

**Outputs of an O–D study:**

| Output | Form |
|---|---|
| **O–D matrix** | Trips from each zone to each other zone |
| **Desire lines** | Straight lines between zone centroids, **width proportional to trip volume** |
| Inputs to the transport model | — |

**The four-stage transport model:**

> **Trip generation → Trip distribution → Modal split → Traffic assignment**

| Stage | Question |
|---|---|
| **Trip generation** | **How many** trips are produced by and attracted to each zone? |
| **Trip distribution** | **Where** do they go — which zone to which? (gravity model) |
| **Modal split** | **By what mode** — car, bus, walk, cycle? |
| **Traffic assignment** | **Which route** — loading the trips onto the network |

**Spot speed study.** Measured by **enoscope, radar, or video**, and analysed by percentile:

| Percentile | Used for |
|---|---|
| **85th** | **Speed LIMIT** — the speed that 85% do not exceed |
| **98th** | **Geometric DESIGN speed** |
| **15th** | **Lower** speed limit; also used in assessing capacity |
| 50th (median) | Average condition |

**Time mean and space mean speed** — a distinction examined directly:

| Speed | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Time mean speed** | The **arithmetic mean** of the speeds of vehicles passing **one PLACE over a period** |
| **Space mean speed** | The mean of the speeds of vehicles **over a LENGTH at one instant** — the **HARMONIC** mean |

> **Space mean speed is ALWAYS the smaller of the two**, and it is the one that enters the fundamental relation **q = k · v**.

The reason space mean speed is smaller is that the harmonic mean weights the **slow** vehicles more heavily — and physically, slow vehicles spend longer in the length, so more of them are present at any instant. Using time mean speed in q = kv overstates the flow.

**Capacity:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Basic capacity** | Under **ideal** conditions |
| **Possible capacity** | Under the **prevailing** conditions |
| **Practical (design) capacity** | With a margin, so the road operates at an acceptable **level of service** |

> **Theoretical capacity of a single lane ≈ 1000 × V / S**, where S is the **average spacing** in metres

and IRC 106 gives design service volumes for urban roads by class and level of service. **Level of service** runs from **A (free flow)** to **F (forced flow, breakdown)**, and design is normally to **LOS B or C** for a rural highway and **C or D** in urban areas.

formulas.label: Nepal road classification — two independent systems
formulas.expression: FUNCTIONAL: National Highway (H), Feeder (F), District (D), Urban (U).   TERRAIN: plain ≤10%, rolling 10–25%, mountainous 25–60%, steep >60%.
formulas.note: Functional class sets importance; TERRAIN class sets the achievable geometric standards.

formulas.label: Road width terms
formulas.expression: carriageway (3.5 m per lane) ⊂ roadway/formation (adds shoulders) ⊂ right of way (whole corridor)
formulas.note: Reserving adequate ROW at the outset is the cheapest and most neglected provision a project can make.

formulas.label: Indian road development plans
formulas.expression: Nagpur 1943–61 star and grid, 16 km/100 km² ; Bombay 1961–81 square grid, 32 ; Lucknow 1981–2001, 82
formulas.note: Radial and circular is an URBAN pattern, offered as a distractor for the Nagpur question.

formulas.label: Alignment requirements
formulas.note: They conflict — the shortest hill route is the steepest. Resolved by minimising TOTAL transport cost.

formulas.label: PCU factors
formulas.note: Essential for mixed traffic. Factors are higher on narrow roads and at high flows.

formulas.label: Design hourly volume
formulas.expression: Conventionally the 30th highest hourly volume of the year
formulas.note: The highest hour would be uneconomical to design for; the average would leave the road congested.

formulas.label: Spot speed percentiles
formulas.expression: 85th → speed LIMIT ;   98th → geometric DESIGN speed ;   15th → lower limit
formulas.note: The 85th percentile is what most drivers judge safe, which is why it sets the limit.

formulas.label: Time mean and space mean speed
formulas.expression: Time mean: arithmetic mean at one PLACE over time. Space mean: HARMONIC mean over a LENGTH at one instant.
formulas.note: Space mean speed is always SMALLER and is the one used in q = k·v.

formulas.label: Theoretical lane capacity
formulas.expression: C ≈ 1000 V / S     (V in km/h, S = average spacing in metres)
formulas.note: Levels of service run A (free flow) to F (breakdown); design to B–C rural, C–D urban.
